cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XVII
The beggar comes to his own house;\nArgus; Antinous' footstool.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
then Telemachus bound the beautiful sandals under\nhis feet — Telemachus, dear son of godlike Odysseus —
and took his strong spear, which fitted his palm well,
straining toward the city; and he spoke to his swineherd:
"Old father, I am off to the town, so my mother\nmay see me. I do not think she will leave off
her hateful weeping and her tearful mourning before\nshe sees me in the flesh. And this is my charge to you:
take this luckless stranger to the city, so there\nhe can beg his dinner; whoever wishes will give him
a crust and a cupful. I cannot carry every man\nwho comes, not I — I have griefs enough at heart.
And if the stranger takes it hard, so much the worse
for him. I like to say the truth of things straight out."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Friend, I have no wish myself to be kept back here.
Better for a beggar to beg his dinner in the town\nthan in the fields; whoever wishes will give to me.
I am no longer of an age for staying on at farmsteads,\nobeying in everything the word of an overseer.
Go on, then. This man will bring me, as you order,
as soon as I have warmed myself at\nthe fire, and the sun's heat comes.
These clothes I have are terribly bad: the morning frost
might be too much for me — and the town, you say, is far."
So he spoke; and Telemachus went out through the farmstead,\nstepping fast, planting evils for the suitors.
And when he reached the well-settled house,\nhe set his spear against a tall pillar, carrying it in,
and went inside himself, over the stone threshold.
And far the first to see him was the nurse Eurycleia,\nspreading fleeces over the inlaid chairs;
with a burst of tears she came\nstraight toward him, and around him
the other slave-women of enduring-hearted Odysseus
gathered, and kissed his head\nand shoulders, welcoming him.
And out of her chamber came watchful-minded\nPenelope, like Artemis, or golden Aphrodite,
and threw her arms around her dear son, weeping,\nand kissed his head, and both his beautiful eyes,
and sobbing spoke winged words to him:
"You have come, Telemachus — sweet light! I told myself
I would never see you again,\nonce you had gone by ship to Pylos —
secretly, against my will, for news of your dear father.
Come now, tell me over: what sight of him did you meet?"
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Mother mine, do not stir up weeping in me, nor rouse
the heart in my breast — I have just escaped sheer death.
No: bathe, and take clean clothing for your body,\nand go up to the upper room with your attendant women,
and vow to all the gods that you will offer perfect
hecatombs, if Zeus may some day\naccomplish works of requital.
And I will go to the assembly-place, to call in\na guest who followed with me as I traveled here.
I sent him on ahead with my godlike companions,\nand told Piraeus to take him home with him
and care for him kindly, and honor him, until I come."
So he spoke; and for her the word stayed wingless.
And she bathed, and took clean clothing for her body,\nand vowed to all the gods that she would offer perfect
hecatombs, if Zeus might some\nday accomplish works of requital.
Then Telemachus went on out through the hall,\nspear in hand; two swift dogs followed with him,
and Athena poured a wondrous grace upon him.
All the people gazed at him in wonder as he came;\nand around him the lordly suitors gathered,
speaking him fair, but brooding\nevils deep in their hearts.
He slipped away from their thick crowd and went\nwhere Mentor sat, and Antiphus, and Halitherses,
who were his father's companions from the beginning,
and sat down there; and they questioned him on everything.
And Piraeus, famous for the spear, came near them,
leading his guest through the town\nto the assembly-place; and Telemachus
did not stand off long from his guest, but went to him.
And Piraeus spoke to him first:
"Telemachus, send women to my house at once,\nso I can send you back the gifts Menelaus gave you."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Piraeus — we do not know yet how these matters will fall.
If the lordly suitors kill me in my halls by\ntreachery, and divide up all my father's goods,
I would rather you keep the gifts and have the joy of them
than any of those men. But if I\nplant death and doom for them,
then bring them, glad, to my house — and glad I shall be."
So speaking, he led the travel-worn stranger home.
And when they reached the well-settled house,\nthey laid their mantles down on the couches and chairs
and stepped into the polished baths and bathed.
And when the slave-women had bathed\nthem and rubbed them with oil,
and thrown about them fleecy cloaks and tunics,\nthey came out of the baths and sat down on the couches.
A handmaid brought water for their hands in a pitcher,
a beautiful golden one, and poured it over a silver basin
for them to wash, and drew up\na polished table beside them.
The grave housekeeper brought\nbread and set it before them,
laying out delicacies in plenty,\ngiving gladly of her store;
and his mother sat opposite, by the pillar of the hall,
leaning back in her chair, spinning fine threads of yarn.
And their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,\nwatchful-minded Penelope began to speak among them:
"Telemachus, I am going up to my upper room to lie\non the bed that has become a bed of groaning for me,
forever stained with my tears, since the day Odysseus
went with the sons of Atreus to Ilium.\nAnd you have not brought yourself,
before the lordly suitors come back into this house,
to tell me plainly of your father's\nhomecoming — if you heard anything."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Then I will tell you, mother, the truth of it.
We went to Pylos, and to Nestor, shepherd of\nthe people; and he received me in his high house
and gave me loving welcome, as a father would his\nson come home at last from far away: with such
kindness he tended me, he and his glorious sons.
But of enduring-hearted Odysseus, alive or dead,\nhe said he had heard nothing from anyone on earth.
He sent me on, with horses and a bolted chariot,\nto Atreus' son, Menelaus famed for the spear.
There I saw Argive Helen, for whose sake the Argives\nand the Trojans labored so much, by the gods' will.
And Menelaus of the great war-cry asked me at once\nwhat need had brought me to shining Lacedaemon;
and I told him the whole truth of it.
And then he answered me with these words:
'Shame on them! Truly in the bed of a strong-hearted man
they want to lie — the spineless creatures that they are!
As when a deer beds down her newborn suckling\nfawns in the thicket-lair of a mighty lion,
and goes questing the spurs and grassy hollows,\ngrazing — and then the lion comes back to his own bed
and lets an ugly doom loose on them both:
so Odysseus will let an ugly doom loose on those men.
If only — father Zeus, Athena, Apollo! —\nthe man he was long ago in strong-founded Lesbos,
when he rose on a challenge and wrestled Philomeleides\nand threw him hard, and all the Achaeans cheered:
such as he was then, let that\nOdysseus close with the suitors:
quick would their fates be then,\nand bitter their weddings.
As for what you ask of me and beg me: I will not talk\naround it, swerving aside, and I will not deceive you.
What the unerring Old Man of the Sea told me,\nnot one word of it will I hide or cover from you.
He said he saw him on an island, in strong pain,\nin the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him there
by force; and he cannot come to his own fatherland,\nfor he has no ships at hand, no oars, no companions
to carry him over the broad back of the sea.'
So spoke Atreus' son, Menelaus famed for the spear.
That done, I came away; and the deathless ones gave me
a breeze, and brought me quickly to my own dear country."
So he spoke, and stirred the heart in her breast.
And godlike Theoclymenus spoke among them too:
"Honored wife of Laertes' son Odysseus,\ntruly he does not know it plainly. Mark my word:
I will prophesy to you exactly, and hide nothing.
Zeus be witness now, first of the gods,\nand this table of guest-right,
and this hearth of blameless\nOdysseus to which I have come:
Odysseus is already in his own dear country —\nsitting still, or moving — learning of these evil doings,
and planting evil for all the suitors.
So clear was the bird of omen I marked as I sat on the\nwell-benched ship, and I cried it out to Telemachus."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Ah, stranger, if only that word might be accomplished:
then you would quickly know my friendship, and gifts
in plenty from me — any man who\nmet you would call you blessed."
So they spoke to one another of such things.
But the suitors, in front of Odysseus' hall,\nwere amusing themselves with discus and javelin throws
on the leveled ground, insolent as ever,\nwhere they always played.
But when it was dinner-time, and the flocks came in
from the fields all around,\nled by the men who always led them,
then Medon spoke to them — for he of all the heralds\npleased them best, and was always by them at the feast:
"Young men — now that you have all\ndelighted your hearts with games,
come toward the house, so we can lay the meal.
There is nothing the worse in a dinner taken on time."
So he spoke; and they rose and went, and obeyed his word.
And when they reached the well-settled house,\nthey laid their mantles down on the couches and chairs
and slaughtered big sheep and fat goats,\nslaughtered sleek hogs and a heifer of the herd,
making their meal ready. And meanwhile from the country
Odysseus and the noble swineherd were stirring themselves
to go to the city; and the\nswineherd began, a leader of men:
"Stranger — since you are set on going to the town\ntoday, as my master ordered — though for myself
I would rather have left you here to guard the farmstead,\nbut him I respect and fear: he might scold me
afterward, and a master's reproofs are hard to bear —\ncome then, let us be off: the day is mostly
gone already, and toward evening you will feel the cold."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"I know. I understand.\nYou order a man who is thinking it too.
Let us go, then — and you lead the whole way through.
And give me a staff to lean on, if you have one cut\nanywhere, since you say the road is treacherous."
He spoke, and slung about his shoulders his beggar's\npouch, full of holes, hanging by a twisted cord,
and Eumaeus gave him a stick that suited him.
The two set out; and the dogs and the herdsmen stayed
behind, guarding the farm.\nAnd he led his master toward the city
in the likeness of a beggar, wretched and old,\nleaning on a stick, with miserable clothing on his body.
But when, making their way down the rugged road,\nthey were near the town, and came to the fountain,
well-built, fair-flowing,\nwhere the people of the town drew water —
made by Ithacus and Neritus and Polyctor;\naround it stood a grove of water-nourished poplars,
circling it on every side, and the cold water ran down\nfrom the rock above; and on top an altar was built
to the nymphs, where all wayfarers made their offerings —\nthere Melanthius the son of Dolius overtook them,
driving his goats, the ones\nthat stood out in all the herds,
a dinner for the suitors;\nand two herdsmen followed with him.
Seeing the pair he broke out against them — named them
in words beyond all bounds, indecent —\nand it stirred Odysseus' heart:
"Now here is the vile leading the vile, no mistake —\nas ever, the god is bringing like and like together!
Where are you taking that glutton, you pitiful swineherd,\nthat beggar-pest, that licker of feast-plates?
He is the sort to stand rubbing\nhis shoulders on many doorposts,
whining for scraps — not for swords and cauldrons.
Give him to me, to keep watch over my farmstead,\nto sweep the pens and carry green shoots to the kids —
and drinking whey he might put some meat on that thigh.
But no: he has learned bad ways, and he will not
set himself to work; he would rather cringe through\nthe town begging, to feed that bottomless belly of his.
But I will tell you this, and it will be accomplished:
if he comes to the house of godlike Odysseus,\nmany the footstools flying round his head from men's hands
that his ribs will wear away with,\npelted through the house."
So he spoke; and passing, the fool, he lashed out a\nheel at his hip — yet did not knock him off the path:
he stood there, steady. And Odysseus weighed it —
whether to spring after him and\ntake his life with the stick,
or lift him by the middle and\ndash his head against the ground.
But he mastered himself, and held it in. And the swineherd
rebuked the man to his face,\nand lifting his hands prayed aloud:
"Nymphs of the spring,\ndaughters of Zeus — if ever Odysseus
burned thigh-pieces for you, wrapped in rich fat,\nof lambs or of kids, grant me this my prayer:
that the man himself come back, and a god guide him home.
He would scatter all those airs of yours, every one —\nthat you now wear so insolently, forever drifting
around the town, while bad herdsmen ruin the flocks."
Then Melanthius the goatherd answered him:
"Well, well! How the cur talks —\nnothing but mischief in him!
One day I will take him on a black well-benched ship\nfar from Ithaca, where he could fetch me a good living.
If only Apollo of the silver bow would strike Telemachus\ntoday in the halls, or the suitors bring him down,
as surely as for Odysseus, far away,\nthe day of homecoming is dead!"
So speaking he left them there, walking slowly on,
and strode off, and came very\nquickly to the master's house.
He went straight in and sat down among the suitors,\nopposite Eurymachus: for him he loved best of all.
The serving-men set a portion of meat beside him,\nand the grave housekeeper brought bread and set it by him
to eat. And meanwhile Odysseus and the noble swineherd
came up close and stopped; and around them came the\nringing of the hollow lyre: for Phemius was striking up
his song among them. And Odysseus\ntook the swineherd's hand and said:
"Eumaeus — surely this is the beautiful house of Odysseus.
Easy it is to know it, to pick out at a glance among many.
One part is joined to another; the courtyard is finished\nwith wall and coping; the double doors are strong
and well-fenced. No man could storm it with contempt.
And I can tell that a crowd of men is feasting in it:\nthe smell of roasting rises, and the lyre
is ringing there, which the gods\nmade companion to the feast."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Easily known — you, who are not\nslow-witted in anything else.
But come, let us think how these things are to go.
Either you go first into the well-settled house and\nslip in among the suitors, and I stay behind here;
or, if you like, you wait, and I go on ahead.
But do not linger long, or someone may see you outside
and throw something, or strike you. Think on it, I say."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus answered him:
"I know. I understand.\nYou order a man who is thinking it too.
You go on ahead; I will stay behind here.
I am not unacquainted with blows and peltings:
my heart is a patient one — I have suffered much evil
from waves and from war. Let this be added to the rest.
But a ravening belly there is no hiding away,\nthat accursed thing, which gives so many evils to men;
for its sake even the well-benched ships are rigged\nto cross the barren sea, bearing evil to enemies."
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And a dog lying there lifted his head and ears:
Argus, the dog of enduring-hearted Odysseus, whom once he
raised himself — and had no joy\nof him: too soon he was gone
to holy Ilium. In the old days the young men took\nhim out after wild goats, and roe deer, and hares;
now he lay neglected, his master gone away,\non the deep pile of dung that the mules and cattle
dropped in heaps before the doors, until Odysseus'\nslaves could cart it off to manure his great estate.
There lay the dog Argus, covered with dog-ticks.
And now, as he sensed Odysseus near him,\nhe wagged his tail, and laid both his ears back flat,
but no longer had the strength to come any closer
to his master. And Odysseus,\nglancing aside, wiped away a tear —
easily hidden from Eumaeus —\nand at once he questioned him:
"Eumaeus — a strange thing:\nthis dog lying on the dung-heap.
His frame is beautiful;\nthough this I cannot tell for certain:
whether he had speed to run to match this beauty,\nor was merely one of those table-dogs men keep,
the kind their masters tend for show alone."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Only too true: this is the\ndog of a man who died far away.
If he were now in form and action such\nas Odysseus left him, going away to Troy,
you would stare at the speed and strength of him.
Nothing escaped him in the deep places of the wood,\nno game he chased: he was surest of all on a trail.
Now he is in a bad way: his master has perished
far from home, and the women are\ncareless and give him no tending.
Slaves — when their masters lose the upper hand,\nthey will no longer do their work as it should be done:
for Zeus of the wide voice takes half the worth away\nfrom a man, the day the day of slavery seizes him."
So speaking he entered the well-settled house and\nwent straight down the hall among the haughty suitors.
But Argus — the doom of black death took him the\nmoment he had seen Odysseus, in the twentieth year.
And godlike Telemachus was far the first to see the\nswineherd coming down the house; and quickly then
he nodded, calling him over. Glancing about,\nhe took a stool that lay there, where the carver would sit
while carving meat in plenty for the\nsuitors feasting through the house;
this he carried and set at Telemachus' table,\nopposite him, and sat down on it himself. And a herald
took up a portion and set it before him,\nwith bread lifted from the basket.
And close behind him Odysseus entered the house\nin the likeness of a beggar, wretched and old,
leaning on a stick, with miserable clothing on his body.
He sat down on the ash-wood threshold, inside the doors,
leaning against the cypress doorpost, which a\ncarpenter once planed with skill and trued to the line.
And Telemachus called the swineherd to him and said —\ntaking a whole loaf out of the beautiful basket,
and meat, as much as his two cupped hands could hold —
"Take these and give them to\nthe stranger, and tell him this:
to go the round of the suitors, every one, and beg.
Shame is no good companion to a man in need."
So he spoke; and the swineherd went when he heard\nthe word, and standing close he spoke winged words:
"Telemachus gives you these, stranger, and he bids\nyou go the round of the suitors, every one, and beg.
Shame, he says, is no good thing in a beggar-man."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Lord Zeus — grant me that\nTelemachus be blessed among men,
and that all his heart desires be brought to pass."
He spoke, and took it in both hands, and set\nit down there at his feet, on the shabby pouch,
and ate, all the while the singer sang in the halls;
and when he had done his meal, the godlike singer ended.
And the suitors raised a din through the hall.\nBut Athena came and stood close by Laertes' son Odysseus
and urged him on: to go gathering\ncrusts among the suitors,
and learn which of them were\ndecent and which were lawless —
though even so she had no mind to\nsave one man of them from ruin.
So he set off, going right-handed\nround, begging from each man,
stretching out his hand on every side,\nas if he had begged all his life.
And they pitied him and gave, and wondered at him,\nand asked each other who he was and where he came from.
And Melanthius the goatherd spoke among them:
"Hear me, you suitors of the far-famed queen,\nabout this stranger: I have seen him before.
It was the swineherd, no other, brought him here;
the man himself I do not know for certain —\nwhere he claims his birth."
So he spoke; and Antinous laid into the swineherd:
"You — swineherd — everyone knows you. Why did you bring
this thing to town? Have we not vagrants enough\nalready, beggar-pests, lickers of feast-plates?
Do you think it a small matter that they gather here
and eat your master's living away —\nand now you invite one more?"
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Antinous — well-born you may be,\nbut that was not well spoken.
Who ever goes himself and invites a stranger from\nabroad — unless it be one of the public workers:
a seer, a healer of sickness, a builder in timber,\nor an inspired singer, who delights with his singing?
Those men are invited the wide earth over; but a beggar —\nwho would invite a beggar, to eat him bare?
No: of all the suitors you are always hardest on the\nslaves of Odysseus, and beyond all on me. But I —
I care nothing, so long as steady-hearted Penelope\nlives in the halls, and godlike Telemachus."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Hush — do not trade long speeches with this man.
It is Antinous' way, forever needling, ugly,\nwith hard words; and he sets the others on as well."
He spoke, and then to Antinous said winged words:
"Antinous — how finely you care\nfor me, as a father for his son,
you who order me to drive this stranger from my hall
with a word of command! May god never bring that to pass.
Take and give to him. I do not\ngrudge it — I order it, I myself.
And have no fear of my mother in this, nor of any\nof the slaves in the house of godlike Odysseus.
But no — no such thought is in your breast:
you would far rather eat it\nyourself than give to another."
Then Antinous answered him and said:
"Telemachus, high talker, temper past\nrestraining — what a thing to say.
If all the suitors handed him as much as I will,
this house would keep him at\narm's length three full months."
So he spoke, and snatched up the footstool\nfrom under the table and showed it —
the stool where he propped his\nsleek feet while he feasted.
But all the others gave, and they filled the pouch\nwith bread and meat. And soon Odysseus was to go
back to the threshold, to taste the Achaeans' free bounty;
but he stopped beside Antinous, and spoke a word to him:
"Give, friend. You do not look to\nme the meanest of the Achaeans —
no, the noblest of them: you have the look of a king.
So it is right that you should\ngive even better than the others —
bread; and I would spread your\nfame over the boundless earth.
For I too once lived in a house among men, a fortunate\nman in a wealthy one, and I often gave to a wanderer,
whoever he might be and whatever need he came in.
Slaves I had past counting, and everything in plenty\nby which men live well and get the name of rich.
But Zeus the son of Cronos stripped it all —\nsuch, no doubt, was his will —
he who sent me out with roving pirates to Egypt,\na long road, to be destroyed there.
And in the river of Egypt I moored my curved ships.
Then, you may be sure, I ordered my trusted companions\nto stay there by the ships and guard the ships,
and I sent out scouts to the lookout places.
But they gave way to arrogance —\nfollowed their own force —
and straightway began to pillage the beautiful fields
of the Egyptian men: they carried\noff the women and small children,
and killed the men. And quickly the cry reached the city.
Hearing the shout, at the showing of dawn the people
came; and the whole plain filled with infantry and horses
and the lightning of bronze.\nAnd Zeus who delights in thunder
threw an evil panic on my companions, and no man dared
stand and face it: for destruction ringed us everywhere.
There they killed many of us with the sharp bronze,
and others they led up alive, to slave for them by force.
But me they gave to a guest-friend\nwho met them there, for Cyprus —
Dmetor, Iasus' son, who ruled Cyprus by his strength.
From there I have come here now, suffering hardship."
Then Antinous answered him and raised his voice:
"What god has brought this plague here to sour the feast?
Stand off there, in the middle, away from my table,
or you may come soon to a bitter Egypt and a bitter\nCyprus — a bold and shameless beggar you are!
You stand by every man in turn, and they give\nrecklessly: there is no holding back, no scruple
in being generous with other men's\ngoods — each has plenty at hand."
Then Odysseus of the many designs drew back and said:
"Well, well. So the wits in\nyou are no match for the looks!
You would not give so much as a\ngrain of salt from your own stores,
you who sit now at another man's table and cannot
bring yourself to take of the bread\nand give it — and plenty is at hand."
So he spoke; and Antinous grew the angrier at heart,\nand glaring from under his brows he spoke winged words:
"Now I do not think you leave this hall so prettily\nafter all — not now you take to insults too."
With that he seized the footstool and\nthrew it, and struck the right shoulder
low, at the base of the back. And he stood like rock,\nsteady: the cast of Antinous did not stagger him.
He only shook his head, silent,\nbrooding evils deep in his heart.
Then he went back to the threshold and sat, and laid down
the well-filled pouch, and spoke out among the suitors:
"Hear me, you suitors of the far-famed queen,\nwhile I say what the heart in my breast commands.
There is no grief in the mind, no sorrow worth the name,
when a man is struck fighting for his own possessions,\nfor his cattle, say, or his silver-white sheep.
But Antinous struck me for my wretched belly's sake,\nthat accursed thing, which gives so many evils to men.
If anywhere there are gods and Furies for beggars,\nmay death's end find Antinous before any wedding."
Then Antinous answered him, Eupeithes' son:
"Sit still and eat, stranger, or take yourself elsewhere —
or for words like these the young\nmen will drag you through the house
by hand or foot, and flay the\nskin from every part of you."
So he spoke; but all the rest were angered beyond measure,\nand one of the arrogant young men would say:
"Antinous — that was not well done,\nstriking the luckless wanderer.
Doomed man! — what if he should\nbe some god come down from heaven?
And the gods do go about, in the likeness of strangers
from far countries, taking every shape,\nand move through the cities,
watching over the violence of men,\nand the good order they keep."
So the suitors spoke; but he paid no heed to their words.
And Telemachus nursed a great grief swelling in his heart
for the striking of him;\nyet he let no tear fall to the ground,
but only shook his head, silent,\nbrooding evils deep in his heart.
And when watchful-minded Penelope heard of it —\nthe man struck in the hall — she said among her slave-women:
"So may Apollo the famed archer strike you, Antinous!"
And the housekeeper Eurynome added her word:
"If an end could only come in answer to our prayers,
not one of these men would live to see fair-throned Dawn."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered her:
"Nurse, they are enemies all, for they all plot evil;\nbut Antinous most of all is like black doom itself.
Some luckless stranger wanders through the house\nbegging alms of the men — his poverty commands him —
and all the others filled his pouch and gave,
but that one struck him with a footstool\nat the base of the right shoulder."
So she spoke among her attendant slave-women,
sitting in her chamber. And meanwhile\nnoble Odysseus was at his meal.
And she called the noble swineherd to her side and said:
"Go, noble Eumaeus. Tell the stranger to come here,\nso I may greet him a little, and ask him
whether he has heard anything\nof enduring-hearted Odysseus,
or seen him with his eyes. He looks a far-wandered man."
And you answered her, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"If only the Achaeans would keep silence for you, queen:
the things he tells would charm your very heart.
Three nights I had him, three days I kept him with me
in the hut — for I was the first\nhe came to, running from a ship —
and even so he never finished the tale of his sufferings.
As a man gazes at a singer, who sings to mortals\nlessons of longing that the gods have taught him,
and they ache to hear him on and on,\nas long as he will sing —
so that man cast his spell on me, sitting in my house.
And he says he is a guest-friend of Odysseus' father's line,\nand lives in Crete, where the race of Minos is.
From there he has come here now, suffering hardship,
tumbled on and on; and he swears he has heard of\nOdysseus near, in the rich land of the Thesprotian men,
alive — and bringing treasures home in plenty."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Go, call him here, so he can tell it to my face.
And those men — let them sit at\nthe doors and amuse themselves,
or here in the house, since their hearts are merry.
Their own possessions lie untouched at home,\nbread and sweet wine: their house-folk eat that,
while they crowd our house day after day,\nslaughtering our oxen and sheep and fat goats,
feasting away and drinking the sparkling wine
recklessly. The most of it is wasted.\nFor there is no man here,
such as Odysseus was, to ward ruin from the house.
But if Odysseus came — if he reached his own country —
quickly, with his son, he would\nrepay these men their violence."
So she spoke; and Telemachus sneezed —\na great sneeze — and round about
the whole house rang terribly with it. And Penelope\nlaughed, and quickly spoke winged words to Eumaeus:
"Go — please — and call the stranger here before me.
Do you not see how my son sneezed on all I said?
So may death be not unaccomplished for the suitors —
for every man of them; not one shall\nslip out of death and the fates.
And another thing I will tell you:\nlay it up in your heart.
If I find that everything he says is true,\nI will dress him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothing."
So she spoke; and the swineherd went when he heard\nthe word, and standing close he spoke winged words:
"Stranger — father — watchful-minded\nPenelope is calling for you,
the mother of Telemachus. Her heart bids her ask\nabout her husband, for all the griefs she has borne.
And if she finds that everything you say is true,
she will dress you in a cloak\nand a tunic — the things you need
most of all. And your bread you can beg through the town
and feed your belly; whoever wishes will give to you."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus answered him:
"Eumaeus, I would tell it all, truly, and at once,\nto the daughter of Icarius, watchful-minded Penelope —
for I know about that man well:\nwe have taken up the same misery.
But I am afraid of this mob of hard suitors,\nwhose arrogance and violence reach the iron sky.
Just now, when that man hit me and gave me pain\nas I went through the hall doing no harm at all,
neither Telemachus nor any other man stepped in.
So tell Penelope to wait in the halls,\nhowever eager, until the sun goes down;
and then let her ask me about\nher husband's day of homecoming,
giving me a seat closer to the fire: for the clothes
I wear are miserable. You know it yourself —\nI begged you first of all."
So he spoke; and the swineherd\nwent when he heard the word.
And as he crossed the threshold Penelope said:
"You do not bring him, Eumaeus?\nWhat has the wanderer in mind?
Is he too much afraid of someone?\nOr shy for some other cause,
here in the house? A shy man makes a bad beggar."
And you answered her, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"He speaks as is right — as anyone\nwould judge who thought it through —
wanting to keep clear of the\ninsolence of these overbearing men.
He asks you to wait until the sun goes down.
And for you too, queen, it is far the better way:
to speak your word to the stranger\nalone, and hear him alone."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"The stranger is no fool. He guesses what could happen:
for I think there are no men anywhere, none among mortals,\nwho plot such reckless evil in their insolence."
So she spoke her say; and the noble swineherd went off
into the crowd of the suitors,\nwhen he had told her everything,
and at once he spoke winged words to Telemachus,\nleaning his head close, so the others would not hear:
"Friend, I am going back, to watch\nthe swine and all that is there —
your living and mine.\nAnd everything here — let it be your care.
Keep yourself safe first of all, and be watchful at heart
that nothing happens to you.\nMany of the Achaeans think evil —
may Zeus wipe them out before harm comes to us!"
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"So be it, old father. Go when\nyou have had your evening meal;
and in the morning come again,\nand bring fine beasts for slaughter.
All the rest shall be my care, and the deathless ones'."
So he spoke; and the other sat\ndown again on the polished stool,
and when he had filled his heart with food and drink,
he went his way to his swine,\nand left the walls and the hall
full of banqueters; and they were delighting in dance\nand song, for already the day had come on to evening.
